**The Keeper of Low Point Light**

Every morning before the gulls were awake, Imogen Scott walked the cliff path with a burlap sack over one shoulder and a stick in her hand. The stick was for turning over kelp. The sack was for whatever the sea had decided to give back.

She had kept the light at Low Point for twenty-six years, ever since her father's knees gave out and the Lighthouse Board offered her the post with a shrug and a pension that barely covered tea. The work was simple enough. Wind the clockwork that turned the lens. Trim the wick. Log the weather at six, noon, and midnight. Polish the brass until she could see her own tired face in it. The rest of her hours belonged to the tide.

The beach below the light was a cemetery of broken things, and most of them were no use to anyone. Bottle necks, rusted tin, the odd plastic sandal. But the sea was patient, and over decades it had been grinding the world's discards into something else entirely. Imogen had learned to look for the soft glow of frosted green, the milky white of old china, and the rare, deep cobalt that made her heart skip like a schoolgirl's.

Her collection lived in apple crates along the back wall of the lamp room, sorted by color and labeled in her cramped handwriting. Greens in one row. Browns, which the locals called "amber" to sound grander, in another. Whites, blues, and the handful of reds she had found in twenty-six years, each one kept in its own small tin.

Visitors sometimes asked why she bothered. A man from the county once wanted to know whether she planned to sell them, and she had laughed until she coughed. "Sell them to whom? The sea already took its payment."

The truth was harder to explain. Sea glass was time made visible. A bottle that had once held somebody's cordial or somebody's gin had been smashed, tumbled through a thousand storms, sanded by ten thousand tides, and returned to her as something smooth enough to hold in the palm of her hand. It had been lost and then made gentle. She found that hopeful in a way she couldn't quite put into words, and so she didn't try.

On the first gray morning of October, she found a piece unlike any other.

It lay half-buried in wet sand near the base of the rocks, catching what little light the dawn offered. It was a shard of cobalt, perhaps the size of a thumbnail, with one curved edge still bearing the faint ridge of a moulded pattern. She knelt, brushed away the grit, and held it up to the sky. Light passed through it the color of a deep evening sky just after the sun has gone.

She sat down right there on the cold stones and didn't move for some time.

Cobalt was rare. Cobalt with a pattern was rarer still. She turned the piece over and over, imagining the bottle it came from. Had it been a medicine bottle, a perfume flask, a child's toy? Who had drunk from it, or thrown it, or simply forgotten it on a windowsill decades ago? The sea had no interest in answering. It only wanted to make the edges soft.

That evening she lit the lamp at dusk as she always did. The great lens began its slow rotation, throwing its beam across the black water in long, measured sweeps. Ships passed, unaware of the woman in the tower below them, cradling a scrap of blue in her hand like a secret.

She thought about the men who had kept this light before her, going back to the first keeper whose name was carved into the lintel above the door. Had they collected things too? She suspected some had. Lonely people often find small ways to keep their hands busy and their minds anchored. Perhaps they had left their own treasures in the sand or tucked into corners of the tower, waiting to be found by someone patient enough to look.

At midnight she logged the weather. Calm seas, light southwesterly wind, visibility excellent. Then, after a moment's thought, she added a line she had never written before in twenty-six years of logbooks.

*One piece of cobalt, found at the foot of the rocks. Kept.*

The next morning, she walked the cliff path again with the sack over her shoulder and the stick in her hand. The tide was low and the sand was silver in the early light. She turned over kelp and bent to pick up bits of green and white, and she kept her eyes open for blue, though she knew she'd be lucky to find another in a lifetime.

It didn't matter much. She had already found the one she needed, and she had written it down.

Somewhere out past the reef, a fishing boat rounded the point and steered toward the harbor, guided by a light that had been burning on that headland for more than a century. Imogen straightened her back, watched it go, and went back to looking for treasure.
